We will use\nprecise language, definitions, discrete representations, small programs or\nsimulations, and tests to move from a question to a defensible conclusion.\nThis is a **Reasoning Odyssey**: the goal is not to memorize vocabulary or\nproduce fluent-looking answers, but to make the journey inspectable.\n\nThis week establishes the habits we will use later. Trust AI less.\n\nAI is useful in DSCT when it helps you explore: ask for an explanation,\nanother example, a question, a counterexample, a test case, or a different\napproach. Treat every answer as a claim to inspect.\n\n## Tiny example\n\nSomeone says: “A person who flips a fair coin twice must get one heads and one\ntails, because the coin is fair.” It sounds reasonable. But “fair” describes\nlong-run chances; it does not force one particular two-flip outcome. `HH` and\n`TT` are possible too.\n\nUse the five-part method to challenge the claim:\n\n- **Sources:** the meaning of “fair” and the possible two-flip outcomes.\n- **Rules / Assumptions:** each flip has two outcomes; fairness does not fix a\n  short run.\n- **Work:** list `HH`, `HT`, `TH`, `TT`.\n- **Check:** `HH` is a counterexample to “must get one of each.”\n- **One-Sentence Summary:** Fairness does not guarantee one heads and one tails\n  in two flips, so the claim is too strong.\n\nThe same check applies to AI output. Do not submit an AI answer as evidence\nwithout inspecting and explaining it yourself. If you use AI later, label the\nuse and retain your own reasoning, tests, and conclusion as the evidence.\n\n### week-01/student/reasoning-method.md\n# DSCT reasoning method — keep this reference\n\nUse this structure whenever you need to make a claim inspectable. It is a\nworking habit, not a new point system.\n\n| Part | Ask yourself |\n|---|---|\n| **Sources** | What definition, reading, data, example, or tool did I use? |\n| **Rules / Assumptions** | What is already known? What am I assuming? What constraints apply? |\n| **Work** | What reasoning, calculation, code, diagram, or test can another person inspect? |\n| **Check** | What could be wrong? What test, second example, edge case, or comparison challenges my answer? |\n| **One-Sentence Summary** | What did I conclude, and how did I reach it? |\n\nWhen stuck, also write **Expected / Actual / Tried**:\n\n- **Expected:** what I thought would happen.\n- **Actual:** what happened, including the exact output or evidence.\n- **Tried:** what I changed or checked already.\n\nA good help request includes both the evidence structure and this short\nhistory. “It does not work” is a starting feeling; it is not yet inspectable\nevidence.\n\n### week-01/student/thursday-activity.md\n# Thursday activity — Make your reasoning repeatable\n\n**In class:** complete on paper or in a local file. Every normal\nweek's one individual reasoning submission is a **Decision Gate**; the\ninternal gradebook category name (`weekly reinforcement`) and the separate,\nlarger Reasoning Odyssey checkpoint objects are not a second student-facing\nweekly submission on non-checkpoint weeks, and a checkpoint week has no\nseparate ordinary Decision Gate submission at all:\n\n`Decision Gate (weekly reinforcement category) 30% + Reasoning Odyssey checkpoints 15% = 45%`.\n\nFarkle + Machine Learning Synthesis is its own third Odyssey-adjacent tier,\ndistinct from both of the above:\n\n`Farkle + Machine Learning Synthesis 5%` (Week 16 only; not folded into the\n45% above).\n\nEverything else is recurring course work or the final:\n\n`8 recurring categories × 5% + technical presentation/demo 3% + course evaluation 2% = 45%`\n(kickoff, Tuesday AI Fluency, the two Professional Minds strands, A3, the\nfolded A4/Show & Tell category, career artifact sequence, and attendance,\nplus the Tuesday presentation and course evaluation) and\n`Final individual reflection 5%`.\n\nTherefore:\n\n`45% Odyssey (Decision Gates + checkpoints) + 45% other recurring work + 5% Farkle + ML Synthesis + 5% final = 100%`.\n\nThe table's direct sum is also:\n\n`5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 3 + 2 + 30 + 15 + 5 + 5 = 100%`.\n\n## Chassis and rotation boundaries\n\nTuesday contains the Monday-Moment-equivalent AI Fluency touchpoint, the\nfirst Professional Minds day (the Wacky-Wednesday-equivalent strand), and the\ntechnical presentation/demo. Thursday contains the second Professional Minds\nday (the Fun-Friday-equivalent strand) and exactly one rotating technical\nactivity. The technical presentation has its own small evidence-receipt\ncategory because it is an explicit Tuesday chassis touchpoint; it is not a new\nfive-day-cadence category.\n\nThe Thursday activity categories are not simultaneous. Pair Reasoning uses\nthe A3-equivalent category on its live weeks; Show & Tell uses the single\nA4-equivalent category (now also covering the retired A7-equivalent critique\nskill) on its live weeks. The category weights are semester-level weighted\ngroups, so each group contains only the objects that exist in its applicable\nrotation. Week 9 is the frozen exception: Thursday is Fall Break and its\npair-style work is folded into Tuesday. Week 14 is the Show & Tell /\nmini-capstone end of the rotation and is also Odyssey Checkpoint 3 (see\nbelow); the two are distinct objects, not a merged double submission.\n\nThe Decision Gate is the evidence receipt for the actual technical work, not\na second unrelated essay. Its package may include sources/rules/work/check/\nsummary reasoning and the active Thursday artifact when that week has one;\nthe Tuesday presentation/demo receipt is recorded in its separate 3% group.\nThe checkpoint group contains three larger Odyssey synthesis packages —\nWeeks 7, 11, and 14 only — and remains inside the 45% Odyssey family. On a\ncheckpoint week, the checkpoint *is* that week's Odyssey submission; no\nseparate ordinary Decision Gate is also collected for the same week. A\ncheckpoint asks the student to synthesize prior Decision Gate/course\nevidence across multiple weeks (what changed, what proved durable, what\nremains untested), not to complete a new technical project layered on top\nof the week's normal work.\n\nWeek 16 Farkle + Machine Learning synthesis is its own **Farkle + Machine\nLearning Synthesis** category (5%), no longer inside the 30% Decision Gate\ncategory and not one of the three Odyssey checkpoints. It is a special\nend-of-semester synthesis of probability/simulation, algorithms, models,\nevidence boundaries, repeated measurement, AI skepticism, and justified\nclaims, graded on reasoning discipline rather than on which Farkle strategy\nwins, coding polish, or compute resources used. Week 17 is the individual\nreflection at 5%; this model creates no comprehensive programming exam or\nReasoning Defense category. The existing `assignments/programming-exam.md`\ntemplate is therefore not used as a grading category until a later explicit\npolicy decision.\n\nExact Canvas/Savnac object IDs, due dates, and per-checkpoint rubric polish\nremain deployment questions. The checkpoint weeks themselves (7, 11, 14), the\nFarkle + ML Synthesis category placement (Week 16, 5%), and the drop-lowest\nregular Decision Gate rule (see the \"Drop one regular Decision Gate\" section\nbelow) are settled by Prompts 315 and 318 and are not open policy questions;\nonly their exact gradebook/compiler wiring remains a deployment seam. The\ncareer artifact sequence is named because the repository contains that real\nartifact family, but its per-week schedule still needs to be published by the\ncourse build.\n\n## Revision, resubmission, and highest-score policy\n\nThis is settled doctrine (Jeremy + ChatGPT, 2026-08-17):\n\n> **Too late, sucker is not the policy. Better reasoning later is still better reasoning.**\n\nFor eligible DSCT evidence-bearing reasoning work — including the weekly\nDecision Gate objects and the Reasoning Odyssey Checkpoints —\nrevisions and resubmissions remain open for as long as the course is open,\nnot just until a nominal due date:\n\n1. **Revisions/resubmissions stay open while the course is open and the\n   submission system can still accept the work.** A later checkpoint\n   occurring after an earlier gate's due date does not, by itself, close\n   that earlier gate to revision. A checkpoint may mark an intellectual\n   milestone; it must not become a gradebook guillotine that removes the\n   incentive to finish or improve earlier work. The only things that can\n   actually close submission are an explicit, separately authoritative\n   course or institutional boundary — e.g. the end-of-course grading\n   deadline — never the mere existence of a later checkpoint.\n2. Each attempt is evaluated fresh for academic quality, on its own merits.\n3. **Lateness never contaminates the academic-quality judgment.** Marker and\n   Coach grade the submitted work itself, with no due/submission timestamps\n   in view. The deterministic late-work adjustment is applied afterward, at\n   the trusted course edge, to that attempt's own timestamp.\n4. That late-work adjustment is the existing shared curriculum default: 1%\n   per 24 hours late, calculated continuously to the second/hour rather than\n   rounded up by the day, with instructor-granted excused-late time reducing\n   the counted lateness. DSCT does not fork or reimplement this arithmetic.\n   The canonical policy lives at\n   `swosu_cs_curriculum/shared/philosophy/late_work_policy.md`, and the\n   canonical deterministic adapter is\n   `course_foundry/course_foundry/late_work_policy.py` (established by the\n   accepted Marker-sidecar late-work integration). DSCT reuses both as-is.\n5. **The student keeps the highest recorded score earned across attempts for\n   that item.** A later attempt's recorded score (its own fresh quality\n   score, adjusted for its own lateness) is compared against the highest\n   score already on record for that item, and the higher of the two becomes\n   the recorded grade. A later attempt can never lower an already-earned\n   grade — at worst it simply does not replace it.\n6. Because of (5), a strong-but-late revision can raise the recorded grade\n   even after a weak on-time first attempt, and a student who resubmits\n   weaker work risks nothing: the earlier higher score simply stands. This is\n   a deliberate incentive for students to keep improving weak reasoning\n   rather than treating a missed deadline or a rough first attempt as a\n   closed door.\n7. Revision means substantive improvement to the evidence or reasoning, not\n   cosmetic polish. Examples: correcting an invalid inference; narrowing or\n   changing a claim; adding stronger evidence; repairing a proof, test, or\n   model; responding to criticism or counterevidence surfaced in Pair\n   Reasoning or Show & Tell; sharpening an evidence boundary or uncertainty\n   statement; adding a discriminating test or counterexample.\n\nIn plain terms for students: due dates matter and help you keep pace; missing\none does not make the work worthless; late work is still worth doing;\nrevisions and resubmissions are welcome for as long as the course accepts\nwork; every new attempt may raise your grade; your highest recorded score is\nthe one that counts; later submissions still receive the same continuous\nlate-work adjustment as any other late work; and substantive revision is\nencouraged because this course values changed reasoning in response to\nevidence.\n\nExact Canvas/Savnac resubmission-window mechanics and the precise\nend-of-course hard-close date imposed by the institutional grading deadline\nare deployment seams, not open policy questions — the doctrine above is\nsettled, and those remain implementation work for the course build. How the\nhighest-recorded-score comparison and the drop-lowest rule below are wired\ninto the gradebook is likewise a deployment seam.\n\n## Drop one regular Decision Gate (settled, Jeremy + ChatGPT, 2026-08-17)\n\nThis is a narrow resilience policy, not a substitute for the revision/\nresubmission/highest-score policy above:\n\n> **Drop one regular Decision Gate:** after each Decision Gate has resolved\n> to its retained highest recorded score across attempts, omit the single\n> lowest regular Decision Gate score from the 30% Decision Gate category\n> calculation.\n\nThe order of operations is fixed:\n\n1. Grade each attempt for academic quality.\n2. Apply the canonical late-work adjustment to that attempt where\n   applicable.\n3. For each regular Decision Gate, retain the student's highest recorded\n   attempt score (the policy above).\n4. Across the student's regular Decision Gates, omit the single lowest\n   retained Decision Gate score from the 30% category calculation.\n\nBecause the drop is evaluated after step 3, a student can keep revising a\nweak gate; if its retained score rises above another gate's, the identity of\nthe dropped gate changes automatically to whichever regular gate is now\nlowest.\n\n**Eligible for the drop:** regular Decision Gates in the recurring 30%\nDecision Gate category only, including a never-submitted regular gate\nrecorded as zero/missing — a missing gate is eligible to be the single\ndropped gate. That does not close the assignment: it remains open for late\nsubmission/revision under the policy above and the canonical late-work\npolicy while the course submission system is open, and a later submission\nthat raises its retained score simply changes which regular gate is\ncurrently lowest.\n\n**Not eligible for the drop:** Reasoning Odyssey Checkpoints (15%, Weeks 7,\n11, 14), the Week 16 Farkle + Machine Learning Synthesis (5%, already outside\nthe Decision Gate category), Pair Reasoning reports, Show & Tell reports, or\nany other non-Decision-Gate category. This rule does not broaden without a\nnew explicit Jeremy + ChatGPT decision.\n\nThe one-drop rule solves a different problem from the policies above:\ncontinuous late work says getting behind should not eliminate the reason to\nfinish; revision/highest-score says better reasoning later can still improve\nthe record; one dropped Decision Gate says one bad week should not define the\nsemester. Deadlines remain pacing signals; this policy does not create a\n`too late, do not bother` incentive, and it does not change the 30% Decision\nGate weight, the 15% checkpoint weight, or the 5% Farkle + ML weight.\n\nExactly how the drop-lowest comparison is computed and applied inside the\ngradebook/compiler (e.g. Course Foundry or a Canvas/Savnac weighted-group\nmechanism) is a deployment seam, not an open policy question — the doctrine\nabove is settled, and the mechanics remain implementation work for the\ncourse build.\n\n### course_metadata.yaml\n# Discrete Structures and Critical Thinking — durable course metadata\n#\n# Tracked source of truth for COMSC-2043's Fall 2026 offering, added\n# prompt 045 (`jeremy_task_tracking/prompts/\n# 045_add_week_at_a_glance_for_other_three_classes.md`) so the shared\n# `course_foundry.course_information_page` generator (built prompt 044 for\n# Computer Architecture, reused here rather than rebuilt) can push a\n# durable Course Information page to Savnac course 4.
